analysis.one_liner: Caps rent at 30% of income for cost-burdened renters and pushes communities to allow more affordable housing.
analysis.headline: A bill to cap rent burdens and push communities toward affordable zoning died in House committee with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a refundable tax credit covering the amount a household pays in rent above 30% of its income, paid out monthly if the taxpayer chooses, based on local fair market rents. It would also require every community receiving federal housing or transportation grants to adopt a strategy for more affordable, higher-density housing — including things like allowing apartment buildings, easing permitting, and allowing backyard units — and would cut off federal transportation money from communities that refuse. Finally, it would let taxpayers defer 20% of their tax refund into a Treasury savings account that gets paid back with interest. The bill never advanced past committee referral and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters who spend more than 30% of their income on rent — roughly half of American renter households — would receive a federal credit covering the gap between what they pay and 30% of their income, delivered monthly if they elect it. Renters in high-cost areas and lower-income households benefit most, since the credit is fully refundable. Over the longer term, renters in restrictive-zoning communities would benefit from more housing supply, and low- and moderate-income households gain a voluntary way to build emergency savings from their tax refund.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable tax credit covering the amount by which a household's rent (including utilities) exceeds 30% of its income, up to the local fair market rent — meaning many cost-burdened renters would owe no more than about a third of their income in rent.
Allows monthly advance payments of the credit during the year, so the help arrives when the rent is due rather than at tax time.

Requires communities receiving federal housing and transportation grants to adopt strategies for more affordable, elastic housing supply — including allowing multifamily housing, easing permitting, allowing accessory dwelling units, and lifting height and parking mandates.
Bans federal transportation projects in communities that refuse to act on affordable housing, giving the zoning requirements teeth.

Lets taxpayers defer 20% of their tax refund into a Treasury-run savings account invested in Treasury bills, paid back with interest — a nudge toward emergency savings for households that rarely manage to save.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would bear the cost of the rent credit, paid for by taxpayers generally. Local governments with restrictive zoning would face new conditions on federal housing and transportation money. Landlords would face new limits on screening tenants, though the rent credit itself would flow to them as paying tenants.

drawbacks.text: The renter credit is an open-ended entitlement: the federal government would pay the gap between local fair market rent and 30% of a household's income, a cost that grows with rents and could reach tens of billions of dollars per year.

Some economists argue that subsidizing rent without also building enough supply can push rents up, blunting the benefit — though the bill's zoning provisions are aimed directly at increasing supply, which partially answers this concern.

Conditioning federal surface transportation money on communities implementing a zoning strategy would be a significant federal intrusion into local land-use decisions that have traditionally been controlled by cities and towns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The renter tax credit would deliver real, immediate help to the roughly half of renter households that are cost-burdened, and the zoning provisions attack supply restrictions that drive rents up. The honest objections: a large new entitlement that routes money to renters without directly expanding supply could push rents up in tight markets, and conditioning federal transportation money on state and local zoning overhauls would face fierce local resistance and legal/administrative complexity. Those are design challenges worth debating — but the bill never got any hearing, debate, or vote, so they were never weighed on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on December 8, 2022 and sent to three House committees, including a subcommittee referral, but none of them acted before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so it never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 8, 2022, less than a month before the 117th Congress ended.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
It was referred to three committees — Ways and Means, Financial Services, and Transportation and Infrastructure — and then to the Highways and Transit Subcommittee; none ever reported it out.
No floor vote, hearing, or markup took place before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and local governments with restrictive zoning keep the status quo; cost-burdened renters get no new relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: landlords and restrictive-zoning municipalities

for.name: Rep. James E. Clyburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 8, 2022, the final month of the 117th Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means, Financial Services, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearings, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan divide ever showed up in a vote — the bill simply had no visible support beyond its author.

industries.note: The rent credit pays landlords' rents but caps what cost-burdened tenants pay out of pocket, and the bill would ban source-of-income discrimination and criminal-history screening — limiting landlords' ability to pick and choose tenants. The credit also funnels substantial federal money to property owners as paying parties.

Zoning reforms like density bonuses, streamlined permitting, and by-right development open up more land for construction and reduce the cost of discretionary review. More building means more business.
Communities that rely on single-family-only zoning, parking mandates, and long discretionary permitting would have to change their rules or forfeit federal housing and transportation grant money.

Monthly advance payments of the rent credit and a new refund-deferral savings program would add administrative complexity around tax refunds, creating new interactions with the paid tax-prep industry that profits from refund-time transactions.
